transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-08-14 16:00 UTC | Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (Apollo - Head of ML), Devon Clarke (Apollo - Infra Lead), Priya Singh (Apollo - Observability), Luca Moretti (Apollo - Data Privacy)

Summary: Quick technical deep dive focused on how Redwood's runtime exposes token-level traces and metrics via OpenTelemetry, how KV cache and batching choices surface in traces/dashboards, and constraints for VPC/on-prem OTLP export. Customer wants concrete Grafana panels, OTLP config snippets, and a bench run to validate p95 improvements with KV cache enabled.

Topics covered: OpenTelemetry exporters, OTLP over gRPC vs HTTP, token.generate spans, span annotations (kv.hit/kv.miss), batch.size metrics, batching latency tradeoffs, quantized int8 exec timings, VPC egress/collector patterns, mTLS and KMS considerations, dashboard templates and alert thresholds.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. Quick intros, then Samira will walk through the tracing model and sample spans we emit in Redwood.
[00:18] Maya Ortiz: Thanks Alex, excited — we have pretty spiky traffic from search autocomplete, so token-level visibility is basically a requirement for us to understand p95 regressions.
[00:30] Samira Patel: Cool. I'll start with the high-level: Redwood can emit OpenTelemetry spans per request, and we also provide token-level child spans. So you'll see a parent span for the generate call and then child spans like token.generate:0, token.generate:1, etc. We tag each span with model.version, seq_len, batch_size and also kv.cache_hit true/false when the runtime serves from KV cache. Apologies if the demo deck had some typos, sometimes OTLP is rendered as OpenTelem in auto notes.
[01:05] Devon Clarke: When you say "KV cache", is that the prefix cache you mentioned in the docs? And where do the metrics live — Prometheus or OTLP traces?
[01:20] Samira Patel: Good question. We emit both metrics and traces. The KV cache is our prefix/KV cache; hits are tagged on spans and we also emit metrics like redwood.kv.hits_total and redwood.kv.misses_total (exposed via OTLP metrics or Prometheus, depends on collector). For token-level breakdowns we rely on traces because metrics alone don't capture per-token latency ordering.
[01:50] Priya Singh: We're running a strict VPC environment — collector must be inside our VPC. Do you support OTLP exporters that can point to our in-VPC collector over mTLS?
[02:05] Jordan Li: Yes — Redwood Private can be configured to export via OTLP/gRPC to an in-VPC collector. We support client certificate-based mTLS; the preferred pattern is to have a local collector (OpenTelemetry Collector) inside your subnet that forwards to your central observability stack. We can provide example collector pipelines.
[02:35] Maya Ortiz: Can you show a sample span payload? I want to confirm what the kv annotations look like.
[02:42] Samira Patel: Absolutely — sample span (abbreviated): span.name = "redwood.generate", attributes = {"model.name":"rw-13b-quantized","model.version":"v2","seq_len":64,"request.id":"abc123"}, child spans: {"token.generate.0": {"duration_ms":2.1, "kv.cache_hit":true}, "token.generate.1": {"duration_ms":3.4, "kv.cache_hit":false}}. In practice the token spans are numerous; we optionally aggregate them in metrics too.
[03:30] Devon Clarke: That token-level noise — do you recommend storing every token span long-term? Our retention costs are a concern.
[03:45] Samira Patel: Not necessarily. Common pattern: export full traces for a 7–14 day window, and sample later to export only traces where p95 > threshold or errors occur. We also provide derived metrics: token.latency.p50/p95/p99 aggregated per model + endpoint, which are cheap and go to Prometheus.
[04:10] Priya Singh: How do you handle batching? Our workloads vary — some queries are single short prompts, others are long seqs. We need to know batch.size distribution impact on latency.
[04:25] Jordan Li: We instrument batch spans too. A parent generate span includes batch.size attribute and a child span batch.wait which records queueing time. You can correlate batch.wait with token latency in traces. In dashboards we include heatmaps: batch.size vs p95 latency, and queue.time percentiles. This makes it easy to tune batching window and weight policies.
[04:56] Maya Ortiz: On quantization: our ops team is worried that int8 quant might give faster throughput but introduce variance in latency. Can you show empirical numbers?
[05:10] Samira Patel: For rw-13b quantized int8 we see throughput improvements ~2.5x in tokens/sec on A100-ish hardware, typical p50 down by ~30–40% but p95 variability can increase for certain long-tail inputs, especially with longer KV cache warm-up. We annotate spans with quant.mode attribute so you can filter dashboards by quantization profile.
[05:44] Luca Moretti: From a privacy/compliance angle, what PII is present in traces? We can't leak user prompts into our central observability stack.
[05:55] Alex Chen: Good point. Redwood supports redaction hooks. You can configure the collector to strip prompt text; our default token spans do not include full prompt text, only hashed request.id and length metadata. For customers requiring strict controls, we suggest keeping the collector inside the VPC and exporting only aggregated metrics out.
[06:18] Priya Singh: Would you send raw tokens to our collector if we request it?
[06:23] Samira Patel: It's configurable, but we generally recommend against sending raw tokens. If needed, it should be enclosed by strong KMS and limited retention and access controls.
[06:35] Maya Ortiz: Show us a sample Grafana panel you recommend for token-level debugging.
[06:42] Jordan Li: Sure — in the shared deck we'll send a panel set: 1) Trace waterfall view with token spans colored by kv.hit, 2) Histogram of token.duration_ms by token position, 3) Batch size heatmap, 4) Rolling p95 token latency time-series by model.version. We also include anomaly alerts: p95 increase > 20% over baseline for 5 consecutive mins -> page oncall.
[07:10] Devon Clarke: For on-prem deployments where outbound egress is restricted, can the Redwood agent write to a local file and the collector pick it up?
[07:22] Samira Patel: Yes, there are multiple transport patterns: OTLP/gRPC over mTLS, OTLP/http, or file-based exporters. The best practice is an in-cluster collector with a file buffer as fallback so you don't lose traces during collector restarts.
[07:40] Priya Singh: How heavy is the instrumentation from a CPU perspective? If we enable token-level spans for heavy traffic it could blow up CPU on the runtime nodes.
[07:52] Samira Patel: We sampled heavily in our telemetry; full token-level spans add overhead ~5–12% CPU and some network egress. We recommend enabling token spans on dedicated debug routes or sampling 1-5% of production traffic, with full tracing for canary/pilot runs. Also batching decisions can be recorded with lightweight metrics to reduce span volume.
[08:20] Maya Ortiz: In our workload we have a lot of small prompts — autocomplete at 15k qps — sampling won't cut it if we need systemic visibility. Any alternative?
[08:33] Alex Chen: For high-QPS but low-latency workloads we advise: 1) aggregate token metrics (counts/histograms) to Prometheus at high cardinality but without full traces, 2) capture full traces only on p95 spikes or errors, 3) set up near-real-time anomaly detection on the aggregated token metrics. That keeps costs reasonable.
[08:55] Priya Singh: Show of hands — how do you capture KV cache miss reasons? Is it network miss, shard eviction, or simply cold start?
[09:06] Samira Patel: We annotate kv.miss_reason: {"not_found","evicted","expired","stale_shard"}. We include kv.load_time_ms as an attribute on the span that experienced the miss, and emit a metric redwood.kv.load_latency_bucketed. This lets you see if misses add significant tail latency.
[09:31] Devon Clarke: If we use Redwood Dedicated, can we keep all telemetry inside our account and never export to Redwood's control plane?
[09:42] Jordan Li: Yes — Dedicated gives you the option to keep telemetry local. For Redwood-hosted, we use our control plane for some aggregated metrics but you can opt out and route telemetry to your collectors only. Private/on-prem deployments are fully self-hosted with no telemetry egress unless you configure it.
[10:04] Maya Ortiz: Let's talk about dashboards/alerting thresholds. What are sensible p95 alert thresholds for token latency?
[10:12] Samira Patel: It depends on the application: for autocomplete p95 token latency < 30ms might be required, whereas for longer-form generation p95 of 300ms could be acceptable. We'll provide a recommended baseline and a template Grafana alert rule set.
[10:34] Priya Singh: Any gotchas with OTLP collectors — e.g., batching in the collector itself influencing observed latencies?
[10:45] Samira Patel: Yes — collector batching and export time can mask short-term spikes. We recommend instrumenting both in-process spans (so you capture raw timings) and collector metrics (to monitor export latency). Also ensure collector export_timeout is tuned to avoid tail latency amplification.
[11:05] Maya Ortiz: For the bench run, we want to see the delta of enabling KV cache + varying batch window from 4ms to 32ms, and quantized vs fp16. Can you simulate that in Dedicated?
[11:15] Jordan Li: Absolutely. Proposed bench plan: run 3x 30-min experiments on a dedicated pool: baseline (no KV, default batching), KV-enabled (prefix cache warmed), and KV+quantized. We'll capture token span traces and aggregated metrics. We'll also produce a spreadsheet showing expected cost-per-1M-tokens at observed throughput.
[11:42] Devon Clarke: How do you compute the expected cost? Do you model GPU utilization per config?
[11:48] Jordan Li: Yes — we model tokens/sec vs GPU occupancy and amortize instance-hour costs. The spreadsheet ties tokens/sec, latencies, and cost to per-call unit economics. We'll send a template you can plug your traffic into.
[12:05] Priya Singh: Are there limitations on sequence length in the traces? Long sequences produce thousands of token spans and the trace size grows.
[12:18] Samira Patel: We cap the number of token child spans by default at 512 per request, and we include an attribute truncated_tokens=true if capped. You can configure caps per deployment, but beware of trace size and collector burden.
[12:36] Maya Ortiz: Any differences in instrumentation between hosted Redwood API and Redwood Private?
[12:44] Alex Chen: Functionally the same instrumentation surface, but Private adds the option to host collectors internally, disable egress, and tighten retention. Hosted will send aggregated telemetry to Redwood control plane unless you opt out.
[12:58] Priya Singh: Is there a standard OpenTelemetry schema you follow so our existing dashboards map cleanly?
[13:06] Samira Patel: We follow semantic conventions and will provide a mapping doc: attribute names, metric names, and example queries for Prometheus and Loki/Grafana. We'll also provide a dashboard JSON you can import.
[13:22] Maya Ortiz: Great. Any hidden costs we should be aware of when enabling token-level tracing?
[13:28] Alex Chen: Main costs: storage/retention of traces, additional network egress if exporting out of VPC, and minor CPU overhead on runtime. We can quantify these in the bench run.
[13:42] Devon Clarke: One last question on SLOs: can your tracing help us auto-detect a model regression after a deploy?
[13:50] Samira Patel: Yes — combine trace-derived token latency metrics with Redwood Optimize's eval hooks. You can set regression detectors on model.version-specific token latency distributions and trigger rollbacks or alerts.
[14:08] Maya Ortiz: OK, that covers it for now. Let's recap next steps.
[14:12] Alex Chen: Recap: Redwood sends OTLP config + Grafana dashboard JSON; Apollo shares anonymized trace and traffic distribution; Redwood runs bench plan and shares spreadsheet. We'll target bench next week. Anything to add?
[14:28] Priya Singh: Please include the example collector pipeline for file-buffer mode.
[14:33] Jordan Li: Noted.
[14:36] Maya Ortiz: Thanks all.
[14:40] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and update the CRM.

End of transcript.
